claim: Doctrine (MDMP) puts COA development before COA analysis (wargaming) and comparison; each COA is screened on five tests (feasible, acceptable, suitable, distinguishable, complete). No opened source measured the validity of these tests. Gap search: still no validity data. A 2004 Military Review article by Klein and Thunholm says research support is weak for the assumption that comparing several COAs finds a better one (d06).
agent_test: Compare agent with and without the five-test screen on the same candidate set at equal tokens; score by downstream plan success.

claim: Doctrine wants 2+ COAs, but under time pressure staffs drop to one COA or produce near-identical COAs (one practitioner report; no counts).
agent_test: Measure pairwise distance of candidates with and without a 'distinguishable' check; report downstream win rate.

claim: An LLM given doctrine excerpts and a mission can write a full COA in seconds; text-only COA-GPT beat two RL baselines on mean reward in one StarCraft II scenario (50 rollouts per variant).
agent_test: Rerun with a second model and scenario; compare to best-of-N with a simulator at equal tokens.

claim: Short human feedback rounds raised COA-GPT mean reward and lowered its variance; best variant stayed 3.4% below the expert human (15 trials).
agent_test: Replace human feedback with a simulator critique string; compare reward after 1 and 2 rounds at equal tokens.

claim: COA-GPT paid for reward with higher friendly casualties than baselines; the expert human had the fewest.
agent_test: Score candidates on a vector (reward, own losses); test whether a loss-aware selector cuts casualties at equal reward.

claim: Adding a map image gave no gain before feedback; only after feedback did the vision variant lead.
agent_test: Low priority for a text agent.

claim: A COA that looks strong against one enemy reply looks weaker when the enemy samples several replies and keeps the best: blue advantage .516 to .485 (best-of-8), .479 (best-of-16); win rate .920 to .820. Offline synthetic benchmark, 50 scenarios.
schema_part: S test against adversary; O red-team
agent_test: Evaluate the agent's chosen plan against best-of-k adversary replies for k=1..16; check selection shifts as k rises.

claim: Static LLM ranking of candidate plans disagrees with ranking from adversarial simulation; plans passing a rule-based check often fail against a learned adversary (mission success 0.72 to 0.86 with multi-agent planner plus adversarial simulation).
schema_part: S test: simulate, do not only judge
agent_test: At equal tokens compare plan choice by LLM self-ranking vs by running a toy opponent simulator; measure agreement and final success. Both sources are 2026 preprints with synthetic or learned adversaries.
audit_note: Only IFPV (listed twice) supports it, on 7 plans from one simulator; Vidra et al. is a synthetic best-response benchmark that does not test static LLM ranking or rule-based checks, and 0.72 to 0.86 is single-step LLM vs the multi-agent planner (MPHA).

claim: Role-specialised councils with red-team critique and revision gave only a small gain over quality-greedy selection (.509 vs .485 advantage); the revision itself barely lowered adversarial pressure (.014).
agent_test: Compare council vs one model with the same token budget (single prompt, k samples).

claim: Choosing the enemy reply by a hand-set doctrine rubric gives about the same pressure as best-of-8 (.488 vs .485) and changes the pick in 56% of scenarios.
agent_test: Test a rubric-weighted opponent reply against free best-of-k.

claim: Scenario framing stored as metadata had no effect on generated COAs until the authors found and fixed it: a benchmark-design failure to guard against.
agent_test: Ablate each prompt section in our harness and confirm the output changes.

claim: Non-LLM generators can build diverse COA pools: genetic algorithm plus learned sequencer gives 20 COAs with MAPE 4.07% against optimal sequencing; best and worst COAs kept rank under 5-20% travel-time noise, middle ones swapped.
schema_part: S3 generate pool; memory of fallbacks
agent_test: Test pool-with-fallback vs single plan under perturbed tasks.

claim: Search-based COA generation (thousands of simulated placements ranked by simulated losses, illegal moves penalised, re-plan as battle changes) works for ground battle in simulation.
agent_test: Use simulate-then-rank as the template for tool-checked candidates.

claim: LLMs cannot reliably fix their own reasoning without outside feedback: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one self-correction round; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after two. Earlier gains used the oracle label.
schema_part: G no unaided self-review; O verify via external check
agent_test: Compare self-review vs external-checker review at equal tokens on plan tasks.
audit_note: Kambhampati et al. adds the argument but no new numbers; 38.1 is after round 1 (3 calls), 89.0 after round 2 (5 calls).

claim: Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at equal response counts (GSM8K, 6 responses: debate 83.2 vs self-consistency 85.3), yet a different paper reports debate gains on Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic (26.0 to 37.0).
agent_test: Run debate and self-consistency at matched tokens on our own plan tasks.

claim: Reasoning models plan well on familiar formats but are fragile: o1-preview 97.8% Blocksworld, 52.8% disguised, 37.3% randomized, 23.63% on 20-40 step plans.
agent_test: Same paper in two lines. Add a plan validator and compare.

claim: LLMs are best used as candidate generators with external critics: about 12% of LLM plans were executable and correct; LLM-Modulo reached 82% on a Blocksworld subset and 70% in Logistics.
agent_test: Count valid plans with and without a verifier in the loop at equal tokens.
audit_note: All numbers come from the Kambhampati/Valmeekam group (the 82%/70% figures are VAL back-prompting results from their earlier paper, cited in the position paper; obfuscated Blocksworld only about 10%); the only outside source (IFPV) does not give these numbers.

claim: Tree-style search over generated candidates beat single-pass reasoning on a puzzle (Game of 24: 4% vs 74%), at higher token cost; another paper argues this is prompt priming.
agent_test: Check against self-consistency at equal tokens.

claim: LLM wargame agents escalate: all five off-the-shelf models raised escalation over 14 simulated days, none de-escalated; GPT-3.5 neutral scenario 10.15 to 26.02 (a 2.56x ratio, which is +156%, not the +256% the paper states).
agent_test: Track an escalation-like score across turns for the agent in a game.

claim: Lower temperature (-38% at t=0.5, -48% at t=0.01) and a de-escalation reflection prompt (-57%) cut LLM wargame escalation; 10 runs per treatment, one extension of the Rivera design.
agent_test: Rerun with another model and check variance.

claim: LLM agents track human wargame action mix only at a high level: of 21 actions, GPT-3.5 matched human frequency on 16, GPT-4 on 10, GPT-4o on 9 (214 experts, 48 teams); persona prompts changed nothing significant.
agent_test: Check whether persona prompting raises candidate diversity in our agent; expect null.

claim: LLM recommendations in crisis scenarios are inconsistent across samples (BERTScore-based score up to 0.73); concrete incident detail lowers inconsistency, anonymisation does not.
agent_test: Use cross-sample inconsistency as a confidence signal; test calibration.

claim: Simulated team dialog before choosing is farcically harmonious with little real disagreement.
agent_test: Compare same-model role debate with forced-dissent prompts.

claim: LLMs fall short of humans on opponent modelling and complex situation analysis in wargames: opponent modelling humans 77.9 to 85.7 vs best models near 49; complex situation analysis 85.9% vs 37.5%.
agent_test: One benchmark across four lines; test an explicit opponent-model step at equal tokens.

claim: Only 20 of 223 AI wargame papers (9%) let the language model both choose actions and adjudicate. Gap search: independent direct evidence says an LLM is a weak simulator (see K33).
agent_test: Scoping count; shows the evidence base is thin.

claim: Escalation of commitment appears in LLM groups more than alone: peer deliberation 99.2% vs hierarchical advisory 46.2% (N=6,500 trials overall).
schema_part: G single decider with critic, not peer vote
agent_test: Test sticking with a failing plan under peer vs critic structures.

claim: Expert option generation: the 1986 Klein abstract (opened) says commanders compared options in under 12% of decision points. The chess replication (N=92, opened) found the first-option quality edge did not appear at lower ratings (F(3,992)=1.73, p=.159; first move picked as best 37.3% of the time). Klein 1995 and Johnson and Raab 2003 originals could not be opened; numbers for them are secondary only (85 handball players; first option better than later ones). The effect depends on expertise, so it has no support for a base LLM in a new scenario.
agent_test: Do not rely on take-the-first. Test one-plan-with-check vs three-plan-compare vs best-of-N at equal tokens on a task with a scorer; split results by problem difficulty.

claim: Premortem and devil's advocacy: the Mitchell 1989 abstract (opened) does not report the often-quoted 30% gain, and its first experiment found temporal perspective had little effect. Schwenk 1990 could not be opened (secondary: devil's advocacy beat expert-only; dialectical inquiry not clearly better). Best human premortem data is a small unpublished thesis (52 cadets, fewer fouls and less fixation, no extra time; premortem vs worst-case gave no difference in count). LLM tests are indirect: InvThink cut judged harmfulness 3.22 to 2.19; anticipatory reflection gave 23.5% vs 22.7% (LATS) on WebArena; a dissenter cut LLM conformity. No LLM premortem test on plans was found. ACH did not remove confirmation bias (Cheikes, still unopened).
agent_test: Add a premortem step to plan selection and compare against a same-length plain 'list risks' prompt and against best-of-N at equal tokens; score by downstream plan success.

claim: Mission-planning agent tests show tool-use loops failing by running out of steps (Mil-SCORE 10-step cap); a two-layer wargame agent with expert documents wins more. Per-model numbers not recovered.
agent_test: Low weight: tables garbled.

claim: No source tests, at equal tokens, whether generating 3 distinct COAs and comparing them beats one plan plus self-check or best-of-N on a planning task. Nearest evidence: Snell et al. found revision wins on easy problems and parallel or tree search wins on hard ones (about 4x less compute than best-of-N when allocated by difficulty); PlanSearch found plan-level diversity beats plain resampling on code with unit tests.
agent_test: Run the three arms at equal tokens on a scored planning task, split by difficulty.

claim: Candidate diversity matters when an outside verifier exists: on LiveCodeBench with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, plan-level search reached pass@200 77.0% vs 60.6% for repeated sampling (pass@1 41.4%), but often lowered pass@1. Idea-space diversity score predicted the gain. No test of this on COAs or without a verifier.
agent_test: Measure pairwise idea distance of candidates and final success with and without a forced-diversity prompt, with a scorer.

claim: GPT-4 is an unreliable world simulator: best 59.9% on non-trivial state changes, 92.1% game-progress prediction with rules (61.5% without), humans 80% vs sampled GPT-4 50% in a normalised check. Errors compound over steps. An LLM should not replace a rules-based adjudicator for multi-step outcomes.
agent_test: Compare LLM-judged outcomes with a simulator on 100 COA-vs-enemy-move pairs; report agreement.

claim: LLM cognitive biases carry beyond geopolitics: in 13,465 admissions-style prompts GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under reject framing; a self-help rewrite prompt removed most biased prompt elements. Escalation bias on non-geopolitical plan selection is untested.
agent_test: Randomise candidate order and framing in the selection step; measure choice flip rate.

claim: Opponent modelling helps when it is a structured module: a trained strategy-evaluation network gave 85.35% improvement over plain LLM planning in MicroRTS, while LLMs lost 100% of games to solver-level engines in Connect Four and chess. No test shows a prompted, untrained LLM opponent model beating static ranking.
agent_test: Compare static ranking, LLM-simulated enemy reply, and a rule-based enemy reply on the same candidates at equal tokens.

claim: No independent replication of COA-GPT on another simulator was found, and no token or dollar cost is reported for it. A Nov 2025 citing paper was about report generation, not COA generation. K03 stays single-source.
agent_test: Run a COA-GPT-style prompt on a second simulator and log tokens.

claim: Direction of the field result: Thunholm's Swedish experiment (as reported by its authors) found one-COA recognitional planning about 20% faster with plans described as somewhat bolder, with no blind quality score; no outcome data support the multi-COA comparison. Authors are the model's proponents.
agent_test: Test one-plan-plus-wargame against three-plan-compare with a blind scorer.
